title: The craftsman's devotion
hookLine: in Japan, a craftsman's lifelong devotion to doing one thing well

cards: A wooden box with no nails in it. The corners meet so cleanly that a fingernail can't find the seam.

Somebody spent a long time learning to make a corner like that, then made it again, and again, a little better each time. In Japanese, the ordinary word for a person who makes things with skilled hands is shokunin.
Some people hear more in it than a job title: a whole way of working, and a kind of devotion. Today: the craftsman's devotion.

teach.h: THE EVERYDAY WORD FOR A MAKER.
teach.b: First, the word. Shokunin is the everyday Japanese word for a craftsperson, an artisan: the woodworker, the knife-maker, the person who makes noodles by hand.

When some people in Japan speak of craftspeople, the word can also carry a sense of character: someone devoted to one craft, refining it over a whole working life, taking the work personally, as a responsibility to whoever will use it.
That second sense doesn't come from a scripture. It lives in how people talk. Second, an old book that honors the same kind of person.
The Wisdom of Ben Sira, also called Sirach or Ecclesiasticus, describes the engraver cutting seals, the smith at his anvil, the potter at his wheel.
The smith, it says, sets his mind on finishing his work and watches to polish it perfectly. The potter is always carefully set at his work. Third, Ben Sira's turn.
These people, he admits, won't be sought for public counsel or sit in the judge's seat. Then he says that without them a city couldn't be lived in.
They maintain the fabric of the world, and their desire is in the work of their craft. Fourth, devotion up close. It isn't perfection on the first try, or pride in being the best.

teach.h: THE NEXT CUT, A BIT CLEANER.
teach.b: It's returning to the same work and making the next cut a bit cleaner than the last, with the attention on the work and the person who will use it.
A bowl, a spreadsheet, a cup of tea, a lesson plan: each can be done the ordinary way, or a bit better.

how: In Japan, shokunin is the everyday word for a skilled craftsperson, and some speak of it as an ideal of patient, lifelong refinement; Catholic and Orthodox Christians, whose Bibles include Ecclesiasticus, and others who read it in the Apocrypha, find a similar honor given to craftspeople in chapter 38.

finishing the work, and polishing it perfectly.

games.why: he sets his mind on finishing his work and watches to polish it perfectly, and Ben Sira says such people maintain the fabric of the world.

practice: Choose one ordinary task, making coffee, folding a shirt, answering an email, sweeping a step, and picture yourself doing it slowly, once, with your whole attention, watching your hands.

Notice one small place where it could be done a bit better: a cleaner fold, a kinder sentence, a corner that meets. Not perfect, just a bit better; if you pray, you can offer the task in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Shokunin. The everyday Japanese word for a craftsperson, and for some, a word for patient devotion to doing one thing well. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: a craftsperson, an artisan. Japanese uses pitch rather than stress, so the capitals are only a guide.

carryVoice: Your line: a bit better. The corner that meets counts, even when nobody notices. Until tomorrow.
